title: Why Does Injustice Go Unpunished?
overview: Job lists the cruelty the powerful inflict on the poor and asks why God seems to let it happen without stepping in.

parts.label: Where are God's court days? (v. 1)
parts.note: Job pictures God as a judge who never sets a date for the hearing. People who trust God wait for wrongs to be put right and never see it happen.

parts.label: The powerful rob the weak (vv. 2-4)
parts.note: Stones marked the edges of a family's land, so moving them quietly stole land, something Israel's law cursed. Taking an orphan's donkey or a widow's ox as security for a debt took the one animal they needed to make a living.

parts.label: How the poor survive (vv. 5-12)
parts.note: Driven into hiding, the poor scavenge like wild animals, sleep cold in the rain, and have children seized for debt, while they harvest grain and press oil and wine for others and still go hungry and thirsty. Even in the city the dying cry out, and Job's bitter point is that God holds no one to account.

parts.label: Those who love the dark (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: Murderers, adulterers and burglars work at night, and in a land of mud brick houses thieves literally dug through walls. For them the dawn is what they fear, the way most people fear the dark.

parts.label: Do the wicked vanish? (vv. 18-24)
parts.note: Verses 18 to 21 say the wicked melt away like snow and are forgotten, which sounds like the friends' view, so scholars are unsure whether Job is quoting them, voicing a hope, or whether lines have been moved. The Hebrew of verses 22 to 24 is hard: some translations say God drags the mighty away, others that he keeps them alive and secure while watching them, and either way they end up cut down like everyone else.

parts.label: Prove me wrong (v. 25)
parts.note: Job dares his friends to show that anything he has described is untrue. He is saying the real world does not match their claim that the wicked always get what they deserve.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether verses 18 to 24 are Job's own words, a mocking echo of his friends, or lines that belong to another speaker, and that choice changes how bleak Job's picture of the world finally is.
think: When you see people get away with harming others, what does that do to your sense of whether the world is fair?
